beats.text: A graduate student spotted it on paper.
beats.note: National Geographic says the first sign was on 6 August 1967, in a squiggly stretch of readout under a quarter inch long, while she was a Cambridge graduate student.

beats.text: They half joked it was aliens.
beats.note: Britannica says the team jokingly dubbed the regular pulses LGM, for Little Green Men.

beats.name: Ryle and Hewish
beats.role: The Nobel press release credits Ryle for aperture synthesis and Hewish for his decisive role in the discovery of pulsars. It does not mention Bell Burnell.

beats.note: Britannica says several protested her omission, though she maintained the prize was presented appropriately given her student status.

beats.context: Her 2018 Special Breakthrough Prize. National Geographic says she is donating it to a UK charity supporting physics graduate students from under-represented groups.

beats.text: She found the pulses. The prize went to her advisor.
